claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially a high-temperature BCC phase.
Cooling rate can alter the phase assemblage of compositionally complex alloys.
Slow cooling gives atoms sufficient time to rearrange locally.
Slow cooling of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 produces local compositional clustering.
Slow cooling of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 produces nonequilibrium short-range order.
Nonequilibrium manufacturing processes can generate SRO states inaccessible through equilibrium thermodynamics.
Local compositional fluctuations and SRO act as heterogeneous nucleation sites.
Those heterogeneous nucleation sites promote metastable-phase formation in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Rapid quenching suppresses local compositional fluctuations and nonequilibrium SRO.
Rapid quenching produces a more homogeneous state with fewer metastable phases.
Slow-cooled samples will have greater local chemical heterogeneity than rapidly quenched samples.
Slow-cooled samples will have a higher metastable-phase volume fraction than rapidly quenched samples.
Rapidly quenched samples will exhibit a more uniform phase distribution resembling near-equilibrium BCC stability.
Controlled intermediate-temperature exposure can lead to precipitation or phase evolution after water quenching.
Extremely slow cooling or prolonged high-temperature exposure will ensure complete diffusional homogenization and near-equilibrium behavior.
Local elemental-concentration mapping can quantify the proposed SRO.
XRD and TEM can be used to compare phase fractions between the cooling protocols.

contradictions.description: The rapidly quenched state is described as resembling near-equilibrium BCC stability, while the conditions field says equilibrium is approached through extremely slow cooling or prolonged high-temperature exposure. This creates an unresolved tension between rapid quenching and the stated route to equilibrium.
